set1.q: Why is a patient with cardiomyopathy referred to cardiology?
opts: Only once symptoms occur at rest

Waiting for symptoms at rest, New York Heart Association (NYHA) class IV, is not the referral rule. Referral is made to establish care, consider genetic testing and review high-risk features. Tell: these are planning and risk-review reasons, which apply well before symptoms become severe.
Only when a device must be implanted

A device is only one possible intervention. Referral is made to establish care, consider genetic testing, review high-risk features and discuss medications or the need for any intervention. Tell: the word only is wrong, because referral serves several purposes.
Only after an admission for edema

No admission for edema is required first. Cardiology referral is made to establish care, consider genetic testing, review high-risk features and discuss medications or interventions. Tell: referral is part of setting up care, not a step that waits for a complication.
To establish care and review risk features

Correct. A patient with cardiomyopathy is referred to cardiology to establish care, consider genetic testing, review any high-risk features, and discuss medications or the need for an intervention. This applies across the three types: dilated, hypertrophic and restrictive cardiomyopathy.

set1.q: Which group is particularly susceptible to acute myocarditis?
opts: Smokers

Smoking is not the named susceptibility; patients typically have no underlying cardiac dysfunction or low cardiac risk. The group singled out as particularly susceptible is young males. Tell: the susceptible group is defined by age and sex, not by a habit.
Young males

Correct. Acute myocarditis has no race predilection and incidence is similar between males and females, but young males are particularly susceptible. Most patients with mild symptoms recover completely, while one third later develop dilated cardiomyopathy.
Older women

Older women are not singled out; incidence is similar between the sexes, and the particularly susceptible group is young males. Tell: think young and male, often with a flulike illness 1 to 2 weeks before the heart failure symptoms.
Infants

Infants are not the group named as susceptible. Incidence of acute myocarditis is similar between the sexes overall, but young males are particularly susceptible. Tell: the typical patient is a young man with a recent flulike syndrome, low cardiac risk and new heart failure.

set1.q: How often is heart muscle biopsy useful in dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: Rarely; not used routinely

Correct. Endocardial biopsy is not used routinely in dilated cardiomyopathy and is rarely useful. It is reserved for recent onset of rapidly deteriorating cardiac function or a history of systemic disease with possible cardiac involvement, such as hemochromatosis, sarcoidosis or amyloidosis.
Always, to confirm it

Biopsy is not needed to confirm dilated cardiomyopathy; it is not used routinely and is rarely useful. Gadolinium-enhanced cardiac magnetic resonance imaging helps identify inflammatory, ischemic or infiltrative processes instead. Tell: biopsy is kept for rapid deterioration or systemic disease.
Routinely, before drugs

Treatment does not wait for tissue: the drug list of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, beta blockers and others is used without biopsy, which is not used routinely. Tell: biopsy is reserved for recent rapid deterioration or a systemic disease such as sarcoidosis or amyloidosis.
Yearly, for monitoring

There is no surveillance biopsy; biopsy is rarely useful in dilated cardiomyopathy and is kept for two indications, recent rapidly deteriorating cardiac function or systemic disease with possible cardiac involvement. Tell: rarely useful rules out a yearly schedule.

set1.q: Which device therapies are part of adult cardiomyopathy care?
opts: Carotid stent or vena cava filter devices

Neither a carotid stent nor a vena cava filter is listed for cardiomyopathy. Adult device therapy is an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator or a biventricular pacemaker, with an assist device or transplant in advanced cases. Tell: the adult devices are cardiac, a defibrillator or a pacemaker.
Temporary external pacing, as needed

Temporary external pacing is not the listed strategy. Adults receive an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator or a biventricular pacemaker, and select adolescents may also receive a defibrillator. Tell: the listed devices are implanted, not external.
Defibrillator or biventricular pacemaker

Correct. Device therapy for adults with cardiomyopathy is an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) or a biventricular pacemaker, alongside guideline-directed drugs and lifestyle changes. A left ventricular assist device (LVAD) or transplant is considered in advanced cases.
Intra-aortic balloon pump for all patients

An intra-aortic balloon pump is not listed, and no device is given to all patients. Adult device therapy is a defibrillator or biventricular pacemaker, while a left ventricular assist device is considered only in advanced cases. Tell: for all patients is the giveaway, since devices are chosen by need.

set1.q: Which laboratory results are typical of Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy?
opts: High lipase and amylase

Lipase and amylase are not part of the Takotsubo work-up. The typical results are an elevated troponin I and T and a frequently elevated B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP). Tell: the presentation mimics acute coronary syndrome, so expect raised cardiac markers.
Raised troponin and peptide levels

Correct. In Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, troponin I and T are usually elevated and B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) is frequently elevated. With ST elevation and wall-motion abnormalities, these results make it mimic acute coronary syndrome until catheterization shows normal coronary arteries.
Normal troponin, normal peptide

Normal markers do not fit: troponin I and T are usually elevated and B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) is frequently elevated. That is why the syndrome cannot be separated from acute coronary syndrome at first. Tell: only catheterization, with normal coronaries, makes the distinction.
High ferritin and transferrin

Ferritin and transferrin are not part of the Takotsubo work-up. Troponin I and T are usually elevated and B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) is frequently elevated. Tell: these patients have chest pain and dyspnea that mimic acute coronary syndrome, so the abnormal results are cardiac markers.

set1.q: When is cardiac catheterization obtained in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
opts: Yearly, for surveillance

There is no yearly catheterization; it is obtained only when a pacemaker or surgery is planned. Risk of ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death is assessed with ambulatory electrocardiogram monitoring for 24 to 48 hours. Tell: catheterization is tied to a planned procedure, not the calendar.
Before any beta blocker

A beta blocker, the initial medication for outflow tract obstruction, does not need catheterization first. Catheterization is obtained only when a pacemaker or surgery is planned. Tell: drugs start without invasive testing; the catheter waits for an invasive plan.
Before a pacemaker or surgery

Correct. Cardiac catheterization is not required for diagnosis of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; it is obtained when invasive therapy, a pacemaker or surgery, is planned. Noninvasive tests carry the rest: cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, exercise echo and 24 to 48 hours of ambulatory electrocardiogram monitoring.
To make the diagnosis

Catheterization is explicitly not required for diagnosis. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging gives good views of the mitral valve and papillary muscles when echo is questionable, and exercise echo assesses obstruction. Tell: catheterization is for planning a pacemaker or surgery.

set1.q: Why may a permanent pacemaker be needed in restrictive cardiomyopathy?
opts: Outflow obstruction on exertion

Outflow obstruction is not a feature of restrictive cardiomyopathy and is not what pacing treats here. The pacemaker is for conduction system disease, because fibrosis of the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes can lead to heart block. Tell: a pacemaker answers a conduction problem.
A low ejection fraction on echo

A low ejection fraction is not the pacing indication, and the drugs used here, beta blockers and verapamil or diltiazem, aim at filling time rather than pump strength. The pacemaker treats heart block from fibrosis of the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes. Tell: pacing fixes conduction, not contraction.
Recurrent atrial thrombus

Atrial thrombi are handled with anticoagulants to prevent embolism, not with pacing. A permanent pacemaker is placed for conduction system disease, when fibrosis of the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes leads to heart block. Tell: clot means anticoagulation; block means pacemaker.
Nodal fibrosis causing heart block

Correct. In restrictive cardiomyopathy, fibrosis of the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes can lead to heart block, so a permanent pacemaker is placed for conduction system disease. Anticoagulants for atrial thrombi and, finally, cardiac transplantation are the other later steps.

set1.q: Which heart sound is often present in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
opts: S4, from a noncompliant ventricle

Correct. A fourth heart sound (S4) is often present in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy because the left ventricle is noncompliant. The rest of the examination fits: blood pressure and heart rate usually normal, pulsus bisferiens, and a forceful, sustained apical impulse.
S3, from a compliant ventricle

A compliant ventricle is the opposite of this disease, where hypertrophy makes the left ventricle noncompliant. That stiffness is why a fourth heart sound (S4) is often present. Tell: noncompliant goes with the fourth sound, so a third sound from a compliant ventricle does not fit.
An opening snap after S2

An opening snap is not described in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The sound often present is a fourth heart sound (S4) from the noncompliant left ventricle, along with a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the left sternal border. Tell: the extra sound comes from a stiff ventricle, not a valve opening.
An ejection click before S2

An ejection click is not among the findings. The noncompliant hypertrophied left ventricle gives a fourth heart sound (S4), and the outflow obstruction gives a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the 3rd or 4th intercostal space. Tell: tie the extra sound to the stiff ventricle.

set1.q: What is the diastolic abnormality of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy without obstruction?
opts: Reduced compliance, high filling pressure

Correct. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy without obstruction, the hypertrophied myocardium resists diastolic ventricular filling (reduced compliance). The left ventricular end-diastolic pressure is elevated, a reflection of that decreased compliance.
Increased compliance, low filling pressure

This reverses both halves. Myocardial hypertrophy reduces compliance, so the ventricle resists diastolic filling and the left ventricular end-diastolic pressure rises. Tell: thick muscle is stiff, and stiff means high filling pressure.
Weak contraction and a huge cavity

A weak squeeze with a large cavity is a systolic problem, but the question asks about diastole, and the hypertrophic ventricle is thick rather than huge. Its abnormality is diastolic dysfunction: reduced compliance with an elevated end-diastolic pressure. Tell: hypertrophy fails at filling, not at squeezing.
Pericardial fluid limiting filling

Pericardial fluid is not the mechanism. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy the thickened muscle itself resists diastolic filling, reducing compliance and raising left ventricular end-diastolic pressure. Tell: the limit on filling is inside the myocardium, not around the heart.

set1.q: Besides valve regurgitation, which complications does dilated cardiomyopathy put patients at risk for?
opts: Arrhythmias and thromboembolism

Correct. In dilated cardiomyopathy, mitral and tricuspid regurgitation develop as the valve apparatus distorts, end-systolic volumes rise and drive further dilation, and patients are at risk for arrhythmias and thromboembolic complications. The impaired contraction leads to systolic dysfunction.
Outflow obstruction and syncope

Outflow obstruction does not fit a dilated, globular ventricle with impaired contraction. The listed risks of dilated cardiomyopathy, besides valve regurgitation, are arrhythmias and thromboembolic complications. Tell: a dilated chamber has nothing narrowing its outflow.
Heart block from nodal fibrosis

Nodal fibrosis is not the listed risk. Dilated cardiomyopathy puts patients at risk for arrhythmias and thromboembolic complications as end-systolic volumes rise and the ventricles dilate further. Tell: the paired risks are rhythm problems and clots.
Plaque rupture and infarction

Plaque rupture is a coronary event, not a listed complication of dilated cardiomyopathy. The risks that come with progressive dilation and dysfunction are arrhythmias and thromboembolic complications. Tell: these complications arise from the dilated heart itself, not from the coronary arteries.

set1.q: Which side of heart failure often dominates in restrictive cardiomyopathy?
opts: Left-sided failure

Left-sided symptoms such as dyspnea, orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea do occur, but right heart failure is the side that may dominate. Tell: hepatomegaly, bilateral pedal edema, ascites and a raised jugular venous pressure point to the right side.
Neither side at all

Filling pressures are elevated in both ventricles, so heart failure is present; right-sided failure is the one that may dominate. Tell: the history lists right-sided signs, hepatomegaly, bilateral pedal edema and ascites, alongside progressive dyspnea and exercise intolerance.
High-output failure

High-output failure does not fit; exercise intolerance here comes from poor cardiac output. Restrictive cardiomyopathy raises filling pressures in both ventricles, and right heart failure may dominate. Tell: poor output plus right-sided congestion is the restrictive picture.
Right-sided failure

Correct. Even though filling pressures are elevated in both ventricles in restrictive cardiomyopathy, right heart failure may dominate: abdominal pain from hepatomegaly, bilateral pedal edema, ascites and an elevated jugular venous pressure. Patients may be more comfortable sitting for the examination.

set1.q: Why is a high degree of suspicion needed to identify acute myocarditis?
opts: It mainly affects older adults

Myocarditis usually manifests in an otherwise healthy person, and young males are particularly susceptible, so older age is not the reason. Suspicion is needed because many cases are not clinically obvious. Tell: the subtle presentation, not the patient's age, is what hides the diagnosis.
Biopsy cannot confirm the diagnosis

Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard, used to establish the diagnosis once other causes of heart failure are excluded, so confirmation is possible. Suspicion is needed because many cases are clinically subtle. Tell: the challenge is recognizing the disease, not confirming it.
Many cases are not clinically obvious

Correct. Many cases of myocarditis are not clinically obvious, with presentations ranging from subtle to devastating, so a high degree of suspicion is required to identify acute myocarditis. It usually arises in an otherwise healthy person and can progress rapidly to heart failure and arrhythmia.
Troponin stays normal throughout

Serum troponin is an indicator of cardiac myonecrosis and is part of the myocarditis work-up, so it is not described as staying normal. Suspicion is needed because many cases are not clinically obvious. Tell: the hard part is thinking of the diagnosis at all.

set1.q: What proportion of patients with mild myocarditis later develop dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: Nearly all

Nearly all overstates it badly, because most patients with mild symptoms recover completely. Only one third later develop dilated cardiomyopathy. Tell: most recover, so the answer must be well under half.
None
The risk is real: although most patients with mild symptoms recover completely, one third subsequently develop dilated cardiomyopathy. Tell: complete recovery for most does not mean recovery for all.
One third

Correct. Most patients with mild myocarditis symptoms recover completely, but one third subsequently develop dilated cardiomyopathy. Young males are particularly susceptible to myocarditis, and there is no race predilection.
One half

One half overstates it. Most patients with mild symptoms recover completely, and one third subsequently develop dilated cardiomyopathy. Tell: if most recover, the share who progress must be under half, and the stated figure is one third.

set1.q: Which region does the hypertrophy of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy most frequently involve?
opts: Right ventricular wall

The right ventricular wall is not the usual site; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is defined as left ventricular hypertrophy, and the region most often thickened is the interventricular septum. Tell: the disease is defined in the left ventricle, with the septum as the favorite site.
Left atrial wall

The left atrial wall is not where the hypertrophy sits; the disease is defined as hypertrophy of the left ventricle, without a causative hemodynamic factor. The most frequent site is the interventricular septum. Tell: the atria are not the hypertrophied chamber.
Ventricular apex only

The hypertrophy can involve any region of the left ventricle, so the apex is possible, but the most frequent site is the interventricular septum. Tell: the word only makes this wrong, and the classic location is the septum.
Interventricular septum

Correct. The hypertrophy of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is often asymmetric and can involve any region of the left ventricle, but it most frequently involves the interventricular septum. It occurs without a causative hemodynamic factor such as hypertension or aortic valve disease.

set1.q: What are the most common symptoms of Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy?
opts: Claudication and pallor

Claudication and pallor are not among the listed symptoms. Takotsubo presents most often with chest pain and dyspnea, with palpitations, nausea, vomiting or syncope. Tell: the syndrome mimics acute coronary syndrome, so expect chest symptoms.
Fever and myalgia first

A febrile, achy start is not described; the precipitant is a significant emotional or physical stressor. The most common symptoms are chest pain and dyspnea. Tell: ask about a recent stressor, then expect chest pain that mimics acute coronary syndrome.
Ascites and pedal edema

Ascites and pedal edema are not the most common symptoms. Takotsubo presents most often with chest pain and dyspnea, and the examination is nonspecific: anxious, diaphoretic, with fast or slow arrhythmias. Tell: the presentation is acute and centered on the chest.
Chest pain and dyspnea

Correct. Chest pain and dyspnea are the most common symptoms of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, with palpitations, nausea, vomiting and syncope also possible. Because it mimics acute coronary syndrome, the examination may look like acute coronary syndrome or acute heart failure.

set1.q: Why must diuretics be used cautiously in restrictive cardiomyopathy?
opts: They worsen iron overload

Iron overload is not the concern; any underlying disorder is treated directly, as the first principle of management. Diuretics need caution because they lower preload, and noncompliant ventricles depend on preload to maintain cardiac output. Tell: the risk is a drop in output.
They thicken the walls

Diuretics do not change wall thickness. They must be used with caution because lowering preload can drop cardiac output in noncompliant ventricles that depend on preload. Tell: the warning is about filling volume, not structure.
Stiff ventricles need preload

Correct. Diuretics treat pulmonary and systemic congestion in restrictive cardiomyopathy, but they lower preload, and noncompliant ventricles depend on preload to maintain cardiac output. Too much diuresis can therefore drop output in a disease that already has the poorest prognosis of all heart muscle diseases.
They cause heart block

Heart block in restrictive cardiomyopathy comes from fibrosis of the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes and is treated with a permanent pacemaker; it is not a diuretic effect. The caution with diuretics is lowering the preload that noncompliant ventricles depend on. Tell: block comes from fibrosis; the diuretic risk is low output.

set1.q: Which serious outcome can the arrhythmias of acute myocarditis cause?
opts: Septal hypertrophy

Septal hypertrophy is a structural change, not an outcome of an arrhythmia, and it is not part of myocarditis. Ventricular arrhythmias or atrioventricular block in myocarditis can cause palpitations, syncope or sudden cardiac death. Tell: an arrhythmic outcome is sudden, not structural.
Pericardial effusion

A pericardial effusion is not an arrhythmic outcome. The danger from ventricular arrhythmias or atrioventricular block in acute myocarditis is syncope or sudden cardiac death. Tell: the question asks what a rhythm problem causes, and that is collapse or death.
Sudden cardiac death

Correct. In acute myocarditis, underlying ventricular arrhythmias or atrioventricular block can cause palpitations, syncope or sudden cardiac death. The heart failure picture may include tachycardia, hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure, a third heart sound gallop, crackles and peripheral edema.
Aortic dissection

Aortic dissection is not a result of arrhythmia. In acute myocarditis, ventricular arrhythmias or atrioventricular block cause palpitations, syncope or sudden cardiac death. Tell: rhythm problems end in syncope or sudden death, not in a torn vessel.

set1.q: Which infection from beta-hemolytic streptococcus involves the heart in 50% to 90% of cases?
opts: Q fever

Q fever is a rickettsial infection, listed with Rocky Mountain spotted fever among rickettsial causes of myocarditis, and is not streptococcal. The beta-hemolytic streptococcal cause affecting the heart in 50% to 90% is rheumatic fever. Tell: match the organism, streptococcus, to rheumatic fever.
Rheumatic fever

Correct. Rheumatic fever, caused by beta-hemolytic streptococcus, affects the heart in 50% to 90% of cases and is among the infectious causes of myocarditis. The other bacterial causes are listed separately: diphtheria, brucellosis, clostridial infections, legionnaires disease, meningococcal infection and Mycoplasma pneumonia.
Lyme disease

Lyme disease is a spirochete infection, listed with leptospirosis among the spirochete causes of myocarditis, not a streptococcal one. Rheumatic fever is the beta-hemolytic streptococcal cause that affects the heart in 50% to 90% of cases. Tell: spirochete means Lyme; streptococcus means rheumatic fever.
Diphtheria

Diphtheria is a bacterial cause of myocarditis, but it is listed with the non-streptococcal bacteria such as brucellosis and Mycoplasma. The streptococcal cause, affecting the heart in 50% to 90% of cases, is rheumatic fever. Tell: only rheumatic fever carries the 50% to 90% figure.

set1.q: Which activity advice has classically been given to patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
opts: Competitive sport if asymptomatic

Being asymptomatic does not open competitive sport under the classic advice, which confines patients to mild to moderate recreational activity in a noncompetitive manner. Sudden cardiac death is the leading cause of mortality in this disease. Tell: the key word in the advice is noncompetitive.
Complete bed rest indefinitely

Complete bed rest is not the advice; patients may keep mild to moderate recreational activity, done in a noncompetitive manner. Tell: the classic advice limits intensity and competition rather than banning activity, alongside staying hydrated and avoiding excess alcohol.
High-intensity interval training

High-intensity training goes beyond the classic limit of mild to moderate recreational activity in a noncompetitive manner. Tell: the advice caps intensity, so high-intensity work of any kind falls outside it, in a disease where sudden cardiac death is the leading cause of mortality.
Mild to moderate, noncompetitive

Correct. Historically, patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy have been told to confine themselves to mild to moderate recreational activity in a noncompetitive manner. They are also advised to maintain hydration and avoid excess alcohol. Sudden cardiac death is the leading cause of mortality in this disease.

set1.q: Which echocardiogram pattern fits restrictive cardiomyopathy?
opts: Big atria, near-normal ventricles

Correct. The echocardiogram in restrictive cardiomyopathy shows marked enlargement of one or both atria, normal or near normal left ventricular systolic function and cavity size, normal or thickened ventricular walls, preserved ejection fraction and abnormal diastolic function. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging helps separate it from constrictive pericarditis.
Dilated, thin-walled ventricles

Dilated, thin-walled ventricles do not fit, because the restrictive echo shows normal or near normal cavity size with normal or thickened walls. The striking finding is marked atrial enlargement. Tell: in restrictive disease the atria are big and the ventricles are not.
Small cavity, septal bulge

A small cavity with a septal bulge is not the restrictive pattern, which has normal or near normal cavity size with normal or thickened walls. Marked enlargement of one or both atria is the key finding. Tell: look for big atria and abnormal diastolic function.
Apex akinetic, base normal

Regional akinesis of the apex is not described for restrictive cardiomyopathy, where left ventricular systolic function is normal or near normal and ejection fraction is preserved until late. The pattern is marked atrial enlargement with abnormal diastolic function. Tell: restrictive disease is a filling problem.

set1.q: Which drug is the aldosterone receptor blocker used to manage dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: Amiodarone

Amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic, not an aldosterone receptor blocker; in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy it reduces sudden cardiac death and converts atrial fibrillation. The aldosterone receptor blocker for dilated cardiomyopathy is spironolactone. Tell: aldosterone receptor blocker means spironolactone.
Spironolactone

Correct. Spironolactone is the aldosterone receptor blocker on the drug list for dilated cardiomyopathy, alongside angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, beta blockers, angiotensin receptor blockers, sacubitril/valsartan, nitrates, diuretics, digoxin as a second-line drug, antiarrhythmics and anticoagulants.
Metoprolol

Metoprolol is a beta blocker, the initial medication for outflow tract obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and belongs to a different class on the dilated cardiomyopathy list. The aldosterone receptor blocker is spironolactone. Tell: the class asked for is aldosterone receptor blocker, and only spironolactone fits.
Verapamil

Verapamil is a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker used for outflow tract obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a negative chronotrope and inotrope. The aldosterone receptor blocker on the dilated cardiomyopathy list is spironolactone. Tell: calcium channel blocker and aldosterone receptor blocker are different classes.

mis.Metoprolol: confused drug class: a beta blocker
mis.Verapamil: confused drug class: a calcium channel blocker from another cardiomyopathy

set1.q: Which drugs may benefit restrictive cardiomyopathy by lengthening left ventricular filling time?
opts: Antibiotics, steroids or antivirals

These are not listed and do not lengthen filling time; the first principle of management is treating the underlying disorder. The drugs that may increase left ventricular filling time are beta blockers and verapamil or diltiazem. Tell: slowing the heart rate is what buys filling time.
Beta blockers, verapamil or diltiazem

Correct. In restrictive cardiomyopathy, beta blockers and cardioselective calcium channel blockers such as verapamil or diltiazem may help by increasing left ventricular filling time, improving ventricular relaxation and decreasing compensatory sympathetic stimulation. They are negative chronotropes and negative inotropes.
Digoxin, epinephrine or norepinephrine

Digoxin, epinephrine and norepinephrine are positive inotropes that increase contractility, avoided in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy because they raise ischemia risk and may induce arrhythmias. They do not lengthen filling time. Tell: the helpful drugs are negative chronotropes and inotropes, the opposite action.
Nifedipine, nitrates or hydralazine

This combination is not the one named. Nitrates reduce preload or afterload and are avoided if possible in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and noncompliant restrictive ventricles depend on preload to maintain cardiac output. Tell: the calcium channel blockers named are the cardioselective verapamil and diltiazem, not nifedipine.

mis.Nifedipine, nitrates or hydralazine: confused drug class: vasodilators that drop preload
mis.Antibiotics, steroids or antivirals: confused treatment: therapy for an underlying cause, not for filling

set1.q: What characterizes restrictive cardiomyopathy?
opts: Transient apical ballooning after stress

Transient apical ballooning after a stressor is not the restrictive picture, which is a persistent problem of diastolic filling from stiff ventricular walls with preserved chamber size. Tell: restrictive disease is defined by impaired filling, not by a regional wall-motion change.
Impaired filling, near-normal chamber size

Correct. Restrictive cardiomyopathy, the least common cardiomyopathy, is characterized by impaired diastolic filling with reasonably preserved left ventricular chamber size and wall thickness that is normal or slightly increased. Ejection fraction stays preserved until late stages, both atria enlarge, and right heart failure is often prominent.
Dilated chambers with thin, weak walls

Dilated chambers with weak walls do not fit; in restrictive cardiomyopathy chamber size is reasonably preserved and systolic function is usually normal, with ejection fraction preserved until late stages. Tell: the restrictive problem is filling (diastolic), not squeezing (systolic).
Asymmetric septal thickening of 1.5 cm

Asymmetric septal thickening is not the restrictive pattern, in which ventricular wall thickness is usually normal or only slightly increased. The defining problem is impaired diastolic filling with reasonably preserved chamber size. Tell: restrictive walls are near normal in thickness; it is their stiffness that matters.

set1.q: Which medication is a recognized cause of myocarditis?
opts: Amiodarone

Amiodarone is not on the list of medications that cause myocarditis, which names penicillin, thiazide diuretics, tetracycline and methyldopa. Tell: learn the drug causes as two antibiotics (penicillin and tetracycline), a thiazide diuretic and methyldopa.
Methyldopa

Correct. Methyldopa is among the medications that cause myocarditis, along with penicillin, thiazide diuretics and tetracycline. Toxic exposures (lithium, arsenic, lead, copper) and autoimmune diseases (systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, myasthenia gravis) are the other noninfectious causes.
Metoprolol

Metoprolol is not among the drug causes of myocarditis. The listed medications are penicillin, thiazide diuretics, tetracycline and methyldopa, with lithium, arsenic, lead and copper as toxic exposures. Tell: the only option that appears on that list is methyldopa.
Lisinopril

Lisinopril is not a listed cause of myocarditis. The medications named are penicillin, thiazide diuretics, tetracycline and methyldopa, and autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus are another noninfectious cause. Tell: memorize the four drug causes; lisinopril is not one of them.

set1.q: Which parasite causes dilated cardiomyopathy through Chagas disease?
opts: Toxoplasma gondii

Toxoplasma gondii is not listed; the only parasite named among the causes of dilated cardiomyopathy and of myocarditis is Trypanosoma cruzi, the cause of Chagas disease. Tell: Chagas disease and Trypanosoma cruzi always go together on these lists.
Plasmodium falciparum

Plasmodium falciparum does not appear among the infectious causes. Chagas disease is caused by Trypanosoma cruzi, listed under parasitic causes of both dilated cardiomyopathy and acute myocarditis. Tell: the infectious causes are mainly viral, with one parasite, Trypanosoma cruzi.
Giardia lamblia

Giardia lamblia is not among the listed causes. The parasitic cause of dilated cardiomyopathy, through Chagas disease, is Trypanosoma cruzi; the other infectious causes listed are viral, such as coxsackievirus and parvovirus B19. Tell: one parasite only, Trypanosoma cruzi.
Trypanosoma cruzi

Correct. Trypanosoma cruzi causes Chagas disease, the parasitic infectious cause of dilated cardiomyopathy listed beside viral causes such as coxsackievirus, parvovirus B19, influenza and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). It also appears among the parasitic causes of acute myocarditis.

mis.Plasmodium falciparum: competing organism: a blood-borne protozoan of another disease

set1.q: How should suspected Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy be evaluated and treated at first?
opts: As acute coronary syndrome

Correct. Takotsubo cardiomyopathy mimics acute coronary syndrome with no initial reliable differences: troponin is usually elevated, the electrocardiogram shows ST elevation and T wave inversion, and echo shows wall-motion abnormalities. So evaluation and treatment follow established acute coronary syndrome protocols, with admission to cardiology.
As a panic attack at home

Treating it as a panic attack at home ignores elevated troponin, ST elevation and wall-motion abnormalities that cannot be separated early from acute coronary syndrome. Early management follows acute coronary syndrome protocols with admission to cardiology. Tell: until catheterization shows normal coronaries, assume acute coronary syndrome.
As viral myocarditis first

Starting from viral myocarditis is not the advised approach. The syndrome mimics acute coronary syndrome, so evaluation and treatment follow acute coronary syndrome protocols until cardiac catheterization, which most often shows normal coronary arteries, confirms the diagnosis. Tell: the dangerous mimic is ruled out first.
As restrictive disease

Nothing here suggests a restrictive process; the picture is elevated troponin, ST elevation and mid and apical wall-motion abnormalities. Early management follows acute coronary syndrome protocols. Tell: the mimic to exclude is acute coronary syndrome, and catheterization showing normal coronaries confirms Takotsubo.

set1.q: What do Kerley B lines on a chest radiograph indicate?
opts: Pulmonary edema

Correct. Kerley B lines are 1 to 2 cm long horizontal lines that meet the pleura at right angles, and they indicate pulmonary edema. In dilated cardiomyopathy the same chest radiograph may also show cardiomegaly, pleural effusions and frank pulmonary edema.
Pleural effusion

Pleural effusions can appear on the same chest radiograph, but they are a separate finding. Kerley B lines are short horizontal lines meeting the pleura at right angles, and they indicate pulmonary edema. Tell: the film lists effusions and Kerley B lines separately, and the lines mean edema.
Pneumothorax

A pneumothorax is not among the chest radiograph findings of dilated cardiomyopathy. Kerley B lines, horizontal lines 1 to 2 cm long meeting the pleura at right angles, indicate pulmonary edema. Tell: this film shows a heart failure picture: cardiomegaly, effusions and edema.
Lung fibrosis

Fibrosis is not what these lines mean here. Kerley B lines are 1 to 2 cm horizontal lines meeting the pleura at right angles that indicate pulmonary edema, alongside cardiomegaly and pleural effusions. Tell: in a failing, dilated heart, the lung finding is fluid, not scarring.

set1.q: Which self-care point is advised in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
opts: Stay well hydrated

Correct. Patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are advised to maintain hydration and avoid dehydration, along with avoiding excess alcohol and keeping to mild to moderate, noncompetitive recreational activity. Sudden cardiac death remains the leading cause of mortality in this disease.
Limit fluids strictly

Strict fluid limits run against the advice, which is to maintain hydration and avoid dehydration. Tell: in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy the instruction is the opposite of a fluid restriction, paired with avoiding excess alcohol and keeping exercise noncompetitive.
Drink more alcohol

Patients are advised to avoid excess alcohol, not to drink more. The self-care points are maintaining hydration, avoiding excess alcohol and keeping to mild to moderate, noncompetitive activity. Tell: alcohol appears in the advice only as something to avoid.
Use nitrates freely

Free nitrate use is not a self-care point; the advice is to maintain hydration, avoid excess alcohol and keep activity mild to moderate and noncompetitive. Tell: none of the self-care points is a drug; they cover hydration, alcohol and activity.

set1.q: Which echocardiogram finding confirms a clinical diagnosis of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
opts: Apical ballooning with a normal base

Apical ballooning is not the hypertrophic pattern. The confirming echo finding is unexplained left ventricular wall thickness of 1.5 cm or more anywhere in the wall, classically septal. Tell: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is diagnosed by a measurement of thickness, not by a wall-motion pattern.
Pericardial thickening on the images

Pericardial thickening is not part of the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy echo. Diagnosis is confirmed by unexplained increased left ventricular wall thickness of 1.5 cm or more, with septal hypertrophy, a small cavity and left atrial enlargement. Tell: the thickening that counts is in the ventricular wall, not the pericardium.
Unexplained wall thickness of 1.5 cm or more

Correct. Echocardiography is the typical diagnostic test of choice, and the clinical diagnosis is confirmed when unexplained increased left ventricular wall thickness of 1.5 cm or more is found anywhere in the wall. The hypertrophy is most often asymmetric, with septal hypertrophy as the classic pattern and a small left ventricular cavity.
Ejection fraction under 35% with dilation

A low ejection fraction with dilation does not fit; in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy the ejection fraction is usually normal and rises above 75% in late stages, with a small left ventricular cavity. The confirming finding is unexplained wall thickness of 1.5 cm or more. Tell: small and thick, not large and weak.

set1.q: What does a normal electrocardiogram suggest when dilated cardiomyopathy is suspected?
opts: It has no value here

The tracing does carry value: because the electrocardiogram is usually abnormal in dilated cardiomyopathy, a normal one will almost rule out the diagnosis. Tell: a test that is usually abnormal in a disease is most useful when it comes back normal.
It makes it unlikely

Correct. The electrocardiogram is usually abnormal in dilated cardiomyopathy, so a normal tracing will almost rule it out. Typical abnormalities include left ventricular hypertrophy, atrial fibrillation, premature ventricular contractions and conduction delays such as left bundle branch block.
It confirms early disease

A normal tracing does not confirm anything; because the electrocardiogram is usually abnormal in this disease, a normal one will almost rule it out. Echo findings such as dilated, thin walls and an ejection fraction below 40% support the diagnosis instead. Tell: normal pushes away from the disease, not toward it.
It points to alcohol

The electrocardiogram cannot point to alcohol as the cause; liver function tests may be elevated in alcoholic disease. A normal tracing will almost rule out dilated cardiomyopathy. Tell: here the electrocardiogram answers whether the disease is likely, not what caused it.

set2.q: Which history precedes viral myocarditis?
opts: A flulike illness 1 to 2 weeks before

Correct. Viral myocarditis follows a recent flulike syndrome 1 to 2 weeks earlier, with fever, myalgia, fatigue, respiratory symptoms or gastroenteritis. Only then do heart failure symptoms appear, such as exercise intolerance, shortness of breath and chest pain, in a person with no underlying cardiac dysfunction.
Chest trauma 1 to 2 days before

Chest trauma is not the history of viral myocarditis; the prodrome is an infection, not an injury. The patient describes a flulike syndrome with fever and myalgia in the 1 to 2 weeks before heart failure symptoms. Tell: a viral cause needs a viral illness, and the gap is weeks, not days.
Years of heavy alcohol intake

Years of heavy drinking is a long, chronic exposure, while myocarditis presents as an acute decompensation of heart failure in a person with no underlying cardiac dysfunction or low cardiac risk. The viral form follows a flulike illness 1 to 2 weeks earlier. Tell: myocarditis is recent and acute.
An emotional shock hours before

An emotional shock hours earlier is not the viral prodrome. Viral myocarditis follows a flulike syndrome, with fever, myalgia, fatigue or gastroenteritis, 1 to 2 weeks before the heart failure symptoms. Tell: look for infectious symptoms and a gap of 1 to 2 weeks, not a stressor and a gap of hours.

set2.q: Why are nitrates avoided in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
opts: They cause complete heart block

Complete heart block is not the problem with nitrates here. Nitrates reduce preload or afterload, and in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy that aggravates outflow tract obstruction and increases symptoms. Tell: the avoid list (nitrates, and diuretics only with caution) is about less filling, not about conduction.
They raise the blood pressure

Nitrates lower preload and afterload; they do not raise blood pressure. That lowering is exactly the harm: less filling aggravates the outflow tract obstruction. Tell: positive inotropes such as digoxin, epinephrine and norepinephrine are a separate warning, avoided because they increase contractility, ischemia risk and arrhythmias.
They thicken the septum further

Nitrates do not change septal thickness; the hypertrophy is the disease itself, not a drug effect. They are avoided because reducing preload or afterload aggravates outflow tract obstruction and may increase symptoms. Tell: the harm is a loading effect with each dose, not structural change.
They worsen outflow obstruction

Correct. Nitrates reduce preload and afterload, and drugs that do so are avoided, if possible, in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy because they may increase symptoms by aggravating outflow tract obstruction. The initial drug, a beta blocker, works the other way, enhancing diastolic filling and decreasing contractility.

set2.q: Why does squatting soften the murmur of obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
opts: It slows the heart to a stop

Squatting does not slow or stop the heart; heart rate is not the mechanism. It increases preload, and more blood in the ventricle reduces outflow obstruction, so the crescendo-decrescendo murmur softens. Tell: the maneuver table sorts murmur changes by preload and afterload, not by heart rate.
It closes the mitral valve early

Squatting does not act by closing the mitral valve early. It increases preload, and the fuller ventricle reduces outflow obstruction, softening the murmur. Tell: the mitral valve in this disease shows systolic anterior motion, which causes a separate holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla.
More filling reduces obstruction

Correct. Rapid squatting increases preload, and anything that increases blood flow in the heart reduces the murmur of obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy by reducing outflow obstruction. Passive leg raising (more preload) and handgrip (more afterload) soften the murmur in the same way.
Less filling increases obstruction

This statement is true but explains the opposite maneuvers: Valsalva and standing decrease preload, and amyl nitrite decreases afterload, which increase obstruction and make the murmur louder. Squatting adds preload, so it softens the murmur. Tell: louder means less filling; softer means more filling.

mis.Less filling increases obstruction: reversed direction: the effect of decreased preload
mis.It slows the heart to a stop: confused mechanism: a heart rate change credited for a preload effect

set2.q: Which condition must be differentiated from restrictive cardiomyopathy because the presentations are similar?
opts: Takotsubo syndrome

Takotsubo syndrome is not on the restrictive cardiomyopathy differential. That list is constrictive pericarditis, singled out for its similar presentation, plus acute pericarditis, cardiac tamponade, valvular disease and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Tell: the named lookalike is a pericardial disease.
Constrictive pericarditis

Correct. Constrictive pericarditis is singled out as the condition that must be differentiated from restrictive cardiomyopathy because the presenting symptoms are so similar. Acute pericarditis, cardiac tamponade, valvular disease and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy round out the differential.
Aortic dissection

Aortic dissection does not appear on the restrictive cardiomyopathy differential. Restrictive disease presents with pulmonary rales, congestive hepatomegaly, hepatojugular reflux and ascites, and the condition that must be separated because of similar symptoms is constrictive pericarditis. Tell: pick the pericardial lookalike.
Viral pneumonia

Viral pneumonia is not on the differential, even though pulmonary rales, congestion and pleural effusions can occur in restrictive cardiomyopathy. The condition that must be separated because of similar presenting symptoms is constrictive pericarditis. Tell: the chest X-ray here shows cardiomegaly from atrial enlargement, a cardiac picture.

set2.q: How is the diagnosis of Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy confirmed?
opts: Electrocardiogram changes

Electrocardiogram changes cannot confirm it: ST segment elevation and T wave inversion are part of why the syndrome mimics acute coronary syndrome in the first place. Confirmation comes from cardiac catheterization showing normal coronary arteries. Tell: a finding shared with acute coronary syndrome cannot be the confirming test.
Catheterization, normal coronaries

Correct. The diagnosis is confirmed with cardiac catheterization, which most often shows normal coronary arteries. Elevated troponin and B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), ST elevation and mid and apical wall-motion abnormalities all mimic acute coronary syndrome, so normal coronaries are what separate the two.
Endomyocardial biopsy results

Endomyocardial biopsy is not part of the stress cardiomyopathy work-up. The sequence is troponin, B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), electrocardiogram and transthoracic echo, then cardiac catheterization to confirm. Tell: the key question is whether the coronary arteries are blocked, which needs a look at the coronaries.
Troponin level above normal

Troponin I and T are usually elevated in stress cardiomyopathy, but a raised level is also what acute coronary syndrome shows, so it supports the picture without confirming it. Cardiac catheterization showing normal coronary arteries confirms the diagnosis. Tell: confirm means the test that separates it from acute coronary syndrome.

set2.q: Adverse ventricular remodeling in dilated cardiomyopathy gives the heart which shape?
opts: Narrow and tubular

Dilated cardiomyopathy does the opposite of narrowing the heart: one or both ventricles dilate, so adverse remodeling produces a globular, round heart. Tell: the name says dilated, and dilated ventricles round the heart out rather than making it narrow and tubular.
Normal-sized, big atria

Normal-sized ventricles do not fit, because dilated cardiomyopathy is defined by dilation and impaired contraction of one or both ventricles, and the remodeled heart is globular. Tell: here the enlargement is ventricular, and mitral and tricuspid regurgitation develop as the valve apparatus is distorted.
Thick septal bulge

A thick septal bulge implies wall hypertrophy, but dilated cardiomyopathy increases total cardiac mass with little or no cardiac wall hypertrophy. The ventricles dilate instead, giving a globular, round heart. Tell: the extra mass comes from dilation, not from thicker walls.
Globular, or round

Correct. Adverse ventricular remodeling in dilated cardiomyopathy leads to a globular (globe or round) heart. One or both ventricles dilate and contract poorly, total cardiac mass increases with little or no wall hypertrophy, and systolic dysfunction follows.

set2.q: What is the mainstay of treatment for acute myocarditis?
opts: Supportive care

Correct. Supportive care is the mainstay of treatment for acute myocarditis, directed toward the clinical scenario. Some patients need aggressive hemodynamic stabilization, and medications are added as needed: vasodilators, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, diuretics, antiarrhythmics and anticoagulation.
Septal ablation

Septal ablation infarcts part of a thickened septum with alcohol (myectomy is the surgery that excises it), a treatment for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, not acute myocarditis. Myocarditis is treated with supportive care directed at the clinical scenario. Tell: myocarditis care is stabilization plus drugs as needed, not a septal procedure.
Early transplant

Early transplant is not part of acute myocarditis management. The mainstay is supportive care, with aggressive hemodynamic stabilization if needed and vasodilators, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, diuretics, antiarrhythmics or anticoagulation as needed. Tell: treatment follows the clinical scenario.
Long antibiotics

Long antibiotic courses are not in the plan; the listed medications are vasodilators, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, diuretics, antiarrhythmics and anticoagulation, given as needed on top of supportive care. Tell: the mainstay is support, with treatment directed toward the clinical scenario.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set2.q: What is the etiology of Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy?
opts: Plaque rupture

Plaque rupture is exactly what is absent: the syndrome mimics acute coronary syndrome, but angiographic evidence of coronary artery disease or acute plaque rupture is not found. The etiology is unknown. Tell: a ruptured plaque would make it acute coronary syndrome, not Takotsubo.
Viral infection

Viral infection is not the cause; the etiology is unknown, and the recognized risk factor is a significant emotional or physical stressor rather than an illness. Tell: the history to look for is a stressor such as the death of a loved one, bad financial news, a natural disaster or surgery.
Unknown

Correct. The etiology of Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy is unknown. What is known is the risk factor, a significant emotional or physical stressor such as the death of a loved one, bad financial news or surgery, and that 90% of cases are postmenopausal women.
Amyloid

Amyloid is not the cause; the dysfunction is transient and regional, principally in the left ventricle, and no deposit is involved. The etiology is unknown, with a significant emotional or physical stressor as the risk factor. Tell: Takotsubo is transient and follows a stressor.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set2.q: Which laboratory marker indicates cardiac myonecrosis in acute myocarditis?
opts: Serum amylase

Serum amylase is not part of the acute myocarditis work-up, which lists a complete blood count for leukocytosis, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, troponin, electrocardiogram, echo and imaging. Of these, troponin is the one named as the indicator of cardiac myonecrosis. Tell: pick the cardiac marker.
Serum troponin

Correct. Serum troponin is the indicator of cardiac myonecrosis in the acute myocarditis work-up. The same panel looks for leukocytosis on the complete blood count and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate that may be elevated, while the electrocardiogram may show sinus tachycardia or arrhythmias.
Serum lipase

Serum lipase does not appear among the tests for acute myocarditis and does not mark heart muscle injury. The marker named for cardiac myonecrosis is serum troponin, alongside leukocytosis and a possibly elevated sedimentation rate. Tell: necrosis of myocardium is read from troponin.
Serum ferritin

Serum ferritin is not on the acute myocarditis test list and does not indicate myonecrosis. Serum troponin does, while the complete blood count shows leukocytosis and the sedimentation rate may be elevated. Tell: the question asks for necrosis of heart muscle, which only troponin is named to show.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set2.q: What is the gold standard for diagnosing acute myocarditis?
opts: Serum troponin level

Serum troponin indicates cardiac myonecrosis, which supports myocarditis but does not establish it. The gold standard is endomyocardial biopsy, used once other causes of heart failure are excluded. Tell: a blood marker of injury is supportive; the gold standard is tissue.
Electrocardiogram

The electrocardiogram may reveal sinus tachycardia or arrhythmias, findings too nonspecific to establish acute myocarditis. Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard. Tell: rhythm findings show the effect on the heart, while biopsy samples the myocardium itself.
Endomyocardial biopsy

Correct. Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard and is used to establish the diagnosis of acute myocarditis once other causes of heart failure have been excluded. It is recommended in acute deterioration of heart function of unknown origin that is not responding to medical treatment.
Cardiac catheterization

Cardiac catheterization with angiography is used to rule out coronary ischemia as a cause of new-onset heart failure, not to diagnose myocarditis. Once such causes are excluded, endomyocardial biopsy establishes the diagnosis and is the gold standard. Tell: catheterization excludes the alternative; biopsy confirms the disease.

set2.q: Which storage disorder deposits iron in heart tissue and causes restrictive cardiomyopathy?
opts: Sarcoidosis

Cardiac sarcoidosis is an inflammatory cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy that forms granulomas in heart tissue; it does not deposit iron. Tell: granulomas mean sarcoidosis, an inflammatory disorder, while iron deposits mean hemochromatosis, the storage disorder.
Wilson disease

Wilson disease is not among the listed causes of restrictive cardiomyopathy, and the question specifies iron. The storage disorder that deposits iron in heart tissue is hemochromatosis. Tell: the listed causes are idiopathic, amyloidosis, hemochromatosis, genetic, sarcoidosis, radiation and chemotherapy.
Hemochromatosis

Correct. Hemochromatosis is the storage disorder among the causes of restrictive cardiomyopathy, with iron deposits in heart tissue. The stiffened walls then impair diastolic filling, reduce cardiac output and enlarge both atria.
Amyloidosis

Amyloidosis is the most common cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy in the United States, but it is an infiltrative disorder that deposits amyloid protein, not iron. Tell: amyloid protein means infiltration; iron means hemochromatosis, a storage disorder.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set2.q: Where are patients with Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy admitted?
opts: Home, no admission

Sending the patient home ignores that troponin is usually elevated, the electrocardiogram shows ST elevation and the picture cannot be told from acute coronary syndrome early on. Patients are admitted to cardiology. Tell: anything managed by acute coronary syndrome protocols is admitted.
To general surgery

No surgical treatment is part of the plan; diagnosis is by cardiac catheterization, and treatment is empiric and supportive, with beta blockers, anticoagulation for a left ventricular thrombus or diuretics for heart failure. Admission is to cardiology. Tell: catheterization and acute coronary syndrome protocols belong to cardiology.
To cardiology

Correct. Takotsubo cardiomyopathy mimics acute coronary syndrome with no initial reliable differences, so evaluation and treatment follow established acute coronary syndrome protocols and the patient is admitted to cardiology. Care is then empiric and supportive, and most patients completely recover.
To psychiatry

Psychiatric admission misses the cardiac problem: the patient has elevated troponin, ST changes and wall-motion abnormalities that mimic acute coronary syndrome, so admission is to cardiology. Tell: until catheterization shows normal coronary arteries, this is treated as acute coronary syndrome.

set2.q: Which drug pair is part of guideline-directed medical therapy for an adult with dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: Beta blocker and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor

Correct. Guideline-directed medical therapy for adults lists angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, beta blockers, angiotensin receptor blockers and diuretics, and both drugs in this pair are also on the dilated cardiomyopathy drug list. Device therapy and lifestyle changes such as sodium restriction and alcohol cessation sit alongside it.
Calcium channel blocker and long-acting nitrate agent

Calcium channel blockers are not on the dilated cardiomyopathy drug list, and nitrates, although listed, are not part of the adult guideline-directed set. That set is angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, beta blockers, angiotensin receptor blockers and diuretics. Tell: each guideline-directed drug is an angiotensin or adrenergic blocker, or a diuretic.
Anticoagulant and antiplatelet agent for every patient

Anticoagulants are on the dilated cardiomyopathy drug list but not in the adult guideline-directed set, and antiplatelet agents are not listed at all, so nothing supports them for every patient. The guideline-directed pair is a beta blocker with an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor. Tell: every patient does not fit drugs given for a specific need.
Digoxin with an antiarrhythmic such as amiodarone

Digoxin is considered a second-line drug in dilated cardiomyopathy, and antiarrhythmics are listed but are not part of the adult guideline-directed set. That set pairs a beta blocker with an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, plus angiotensin receptor blockers and diuretics. Tell: a second-line drug is never the guideline-directed core.

set2.q: What is the leading cause of mortality in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
opts: Endocarditis

Endocarditis is not described as a cause of death in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The leading cause of mortality is sudden cardiac death, while heart failure symptoms progress gradually and may need transplantation if unresponsive to therapy. Tell: the feared outcome in this disease is sudden, not infectious.
Sudden cardiac death

Correct. The clinical course of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy varies and heart failure symptoms gradually progress, but sudden cardiac death is the leading cause of mortality. That is why patients are told to keep to mild to moderate noncompetitive activity, stay hydrated and avoid excess alcohol.
Aortic dissection

Aortic dissection is not part of the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy course. Sudden cardiac death leads mortality, with heart failure symptoms progressing gradually in others. Tell: the advice to keep to mild, noncompetitive activity exists because the main danger is sudden death.
Embolic stroke

Embolic stroke is not named as the leading killer; the leading cause of mortality in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is sudden cardiac death. Heart failure progresses gradually and may need transplantation if unresponsive to conventional therapy. Tell: the advice against competitive exertion and dehydration targets sudden death.

set2.q: Why are both atria enlarged in restrictive cardiomyopathy?
opts: Leaking mitral leaflets

A leaking mitral valve is not the mechanism; restrictive cardiomyopathy is a disease of the ventricular wall, which stiffens and impairs diastolic filling. Bilateral atrial enlargement follows from that impaired filling. Tell: the cause sits in the stiff ventricles, and both atria enlarge in response.
Septal outflow blockage

Outflow obstruction is not part of restrictive cardiomyopathy, where ventricular wall thickness is normal or only slightly increased and chamber size is preserved. The atria enlarge because stiff ventricles impair diastolic filling. Tell: restrictive disease is a filling problem with systolic function usually normal.
Fluid around the heart

Pericardial fluid is not the mechanism. Restrictive cardiomyopathy is a problem of the myocardium: stiff ventricular walls impair diastolic filling and reduce cardiac output, and both atria enlarge from that impaired filling. Tell: the restriction is in the ventricular wall itself, not around the heart.
Impaired ventricular filling

Correct. In restrictive cardiomyopathy, ventricular wall stiffness impairs diastolic filling, so both atria enlarge as they push blood into ventricles that resist filling. Chamber size and systolic function stay reasonably preserved, and atrial fibrillation is common.

set2.q: When is an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator indicated in dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: Any reduced ejection fraction at diagnosis

A reduced ejection fraction at diagnosis is not enough; medical therapy comes first. The device is indicated only if the ejection fraction is still below 35% after maximum medical therapy. Tell: the indication has two parts, a value below 35% and failure of maximal drug treatment.
After a first episode of atrial fibrillation

Atrial fibrillation alone does not trigger an implantable defibrillator; antiarrhythmics and anticoagulants are on the dilated cardiomyopathy drug list for that. The device indication is an ejection fraction below 35% after maximum medical therapy. Tell: the threshold is pump function, not an atrial rhythm.
When the pulse pressure becomes narrow

A narrow pulse pressure is an examination finding, not a device criterion. The implantable defibrillator is indicated when the ejection fraction is below 35% after maximum medical therapy, while a biventricular pacemaker serves moderately severe left-sided dysfunction. Tell: the trigger is a measured ejection fraction on full treatment.
Ejection fraction below 35% on maximal therapy

Correct. An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) is placed in dilated cardiomyopathy if the ejection fraction remains below 35% after maximum medical therapy. A biventricular ICD combines it with the biventricular pacemaker used for moderately severe left-sided ventricular dysfunction.

set2.q: Where do prominent Q waves appear on the electrocardiogram in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
opts: No lead shows Q waves

Q waves are a recognized electrocardiogram finding in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, prominent in the inferior and lateral leads because the hypertrophied septum depolarizes abnormally. Tell: the thick septum is what produces them, along with left ventricular hypertrophy and left axis deviation.
Inferior and lateral leads

Correct. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, prominent Q waves appear in the inferior leads (II, III and aVF) and the lateral leads (I, aVL and V4 to V6). They reflect septal depolarization of hypertrophied, myopathic tissue and sit alongside left ventricular hypertrophy, atrial enlargement and left axis deviation.
Right precordial leads only

The Q waves are not confined to the right precordial leads. They are prominent inferiorly (II, III and aVF) and laterally (I, aVL and V4 to V6), reflecting septal depolarization of hypertrophied tissue. Tell: remember inferior plus lateral, with left axis deviation.
Anterior leads V1 to V3 only

Leads V1 to V3 are not where the pattern sits. The prominent Q waves of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy appear in the inferior leads II, III and aVF and the lateral leads I, aVL and V4 to V6. Tell: the lateral set starts at V4, so V1 to V3 fall outside it.

set2.q: What is systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve?
opts: Valve ring stretching as the ventricle dilates

A ring stretched by a dilating ventricle is the wrong setting; systolic anterior motion occurs in obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, where septal hypertrophy narrows the outflow tract. Fast turbulent flow then pulls the anterior leaflet into that tract. Tell: the cause is flow through a narrowed outflow tract, not a large ventricle.
Leaflets thickened by old rheumatic scarring

Systolic anterior motion has nothing to do with scarred, thickened leaflets; it is a dynamic event in each systole. High-velocity turbulent flow through the narrowed outflow tract pulls the anterior leaflet forward. Tell: this is a moving leaflet dragged by flow, not a damaged one.
Anterior leaflet pulled into the outflow tract

Correct. In obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, septal hypertrophy narrows the subaortic outflow tract, and high-velocity turbulent flow pulls the anterior mitral leaflet into the flow tract. That causes mid-systolic obstruction of flow through the left ventricular outflow tract.
Posterior leaflet prolapsing into the atrium

The motion is anterior, toward the outflow tract, and involves the anterior leaflet, not a posterior leaflet falling back into the atrium. Turbulent flow drags that leaflet into the left ventricular outflow tract, causing mid-systolic obstruction. Tell: the name says it all: systolic, anterior, into the outflow tract.

set2.q: What is the first principle of managing restrictive cardiomyopathy?
opts: Surgical septal myectomy

Septal myectomy is not part of restrictive cardiomyopathy management; the listed steps are treating the underlying disorder, cautious diuretics, beta blockers or cardioselective calcium channel blockers, anticoagulants, a permanent pacemaker and transplantation. Tell: no step removes heart muscle, because the problem is noncompliant ventricles.
High-dose diuresis first

Diuretics are used for pulmonary and systemic congestion, but with caution, because they lower preload and noncompliant ventricles depend on preload to maintain cardiac output. High-dose diuresis as the opening move risks dropping output. Tell: in restrictive disease preload is protected, and the cause is treated first.
Immediate transplantation

Cardiac transplantation is on the list but is the last step, not the first principle. Management starts with treating the underlying disorder, then diuretics, rate-slowing drugs, anticoagulants and a pacemaker as needed. Tell: restrictive disease has the poorest prognosis of all heart muscle diseases, yet the cause is still treated first.
Treat the underlying disorder

Correct. Management of restrictive cardiomyopathy starts with treating the underlying disorder. Support follows as needed: diuretics with caution for congestion, beta blockers or verapamil and diltiazem to lengthen filling time, anticoagulants for atrial thrombi, a pacemaker for conduction disease and, at the end, transplantation.

set2.q: What produces the third heart sound in dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: Mitral leaflet striking the septum

The mitral leaflet striking the septum is not how this sound arises. In dilated cardiomyopathy the mitral problem is regurgitation, a holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the left axilla, while the gallop comes from blood striking a very compliant ventricle. Tell: the gallop marks volume overload.
Blood striking a compliant ventricle

Correct. The third heart sound (S3) gallop of dilated cardiomyopathy is produced by a large amount of blood striking a very compliant left ventricle, a sign of volume overload. It sits with the other cardiac findings: a laterally displaced point of maximal impulse, regurgitant murmurs and jugular vein distention.
Atrium contracting on a stiff ventricle

An atrium contracting against a stiff ventricle does not fit dilated cardiomyopathy, whose left ventricle is very compliant and volume overloaded. The third heart sound comes from a large amount of blood striking that compliant ventricle. Tell: stiff points away from dilated disease; compliant and overloaded points toward it.
Closure of a thickened aortic valve

Aortic valve closure is not the source, and a thickened aortic valve is not part of dilated cardiomyopathy, whose murmurs are mitral and tricuspid regurgitation. The third heart sound gallop is a large amount of blood striking a very compliant left ventricle. Tell: the gallop marks volume overload, not a valve.

set2.q: Which description fits the ventricles in dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: Stiff, with near-normal cavity size

Stiff walls with a near-normal cavity do not fit: dilated cardiomyopathy enlarges one or both ventricles and weakens their contraction, causing systolic dysfunction. Tell: here the cavity is large and the squeeze is poor, with mitral and tricuspid regurgitation as the valve apparatus distorts.
Ballooned apex that later recovers

A ballooned apex that later recovers describes a transient process, while dilated cardiomyopathy progresses: rising end-systolic volumes cause further dilation and dysfunction, with arrhythmia and thromboembolic risk. Tell: dilation involves one or both ventricles as a whole, giving a globular heart.
Dilated, with impaired contraction

Correct. Dilated cardiomyopathy is characterized by dilation and impaired contraction of one or both ventricles, which leads to systolic dysfunction. Total cardiac mass rises with little or no wall hypertrophy, the heart becomes globular, and rising end-systolic volumes drive further dilation.
Thick-walled, with a small cavity

Thick walls around a small cavity are the reverse of this disease, which increases cardiac mass with little or no wall hypertrophy while the ventricles dilate. Tell: dilated means a large chamber with impaired contraction and systolic dysfunction.

set2.q: What does gadolinium add to magnetic resonance imaging in suspected myocarditis?
opts: Rules out coronary blockage

Ruling out coronary disease is the job of cardiac angiography, which excludes coronary ischemia as a cause of new-onset heart failure. Gadolinium in magnetic resonance imaging improves the visibility of inflammation and its extent. Tell: angiography looks at the coronaries; gadolinium imaging looks at inflamed muscle.
Measures troponin release

Troponin is a serum blood test, the indicator of cardiac myonecrosis, and is not measured by imaging. Gadolinium improves the visibility and extent of inflammation on magnetic resonance imaging. Tell: necrosis is measured in blood; inflammation is shown on enhanced imaging.
Grows the causative virus

Magnetic resonance imaging cannot grow or identify a virus. Gadolinium improves the visibility and extent of inflammation, and the tissue diagnosis comes from endomyocardial biopsy, the gold standard. Tell: imaging shows where and how much inflammation; biopsy establishes the diagnosis.
Shows the extent of inflammation

Correct. In suspected myocarditis, gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) improves the visibility of inflammation and shows its extent in the myocardium. It sits in the work-up beside troponin, the electrocardiogram, echo and angiography, with endomyocardial biopsy as the gold standard.

set2.q: What is the risk factor for Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy?
opts: A major emotional or physical stressor

Correct. The risk factor for Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is a significant emotional or physical stressor, such as the death of a loved one, bad financial news, a natural disaster, a new diagnosis, surgery, drug withdrawal or near drowning. About 90% of cases are postmenopausal women, who tend to have few cardiac risk factors.
Many traditional cardiac risk factors

Patients with Takotsubo cardiomyopathy tend to have low or no cardiac risk factors, such as hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking or a positive family history. The risk factor is a significant emotional or physical stressor. Tell: a low-risk patient with chest pain after a shock fits Takotsubo.
A flulike illness 1 to 2 weeks before

A flulike illness is not the trigger. Takotsubo follows a significant emotional or physical stressor, such as the death of a loved one, bad financial news or surgery, and its etiology is unknown. Tell: ask about a recent shock or major physical stress, not an infection.
Inherited sarcomere gene mutation

An inherited gene mutation is not described; the etiology of Takotsubo is unknown, and the risk factor is a significant emotional or physical stressor. Tell: Takotsubo is acquired after an event, with 90% of cases in postmenopausal women, rather than carried in the family.

set2.q: What happens to ejection fraction in late-stage hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
opts: It rises above 75%

Correct. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy the ejection fraction is usually normal, but in late stages it rises above 75% because the small-volume ventricle nearly empties to maintain cardiac output. Echo also shows septal hypertrophy, a small left ventricular cavity and left atrial enlargement.
It falls below 25%

A very low ejection fraction does not fit the small, hypertrophied left ventricular cavity of this disease. Its ejection fraction is usually normal and rises above 75% in late stages as the small ventricle nearly empties. Tell: a small, thick ventricle pushes the value up, not down.
It swings every beat

Beat-to-beat swings are not the described change. The small left ventricular cavity nearly empties to maintain cardiac output, so the ejection fraction becomes elevated above 75% in late stages. Tell: the late change is a sustained rise, not variability.
It stays at exactly 60%

The ejection fraction does not stay fixed. It is usually normal early on, then becomes elevated above 75% in late stages because the small-volume ventricle nearly empties to maintain cardiac output. Tell: the late-stage change is upward.

set2.q: Which laboratory test evaluates for anemia in suspected dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: Complete blood count

Correct. The complete blood count (CBC) is the test that evaluates for anemia in suspected dilated cardiomyopathy. The rest of the initial panel has its own targets: a comprehensive metabolic panel for electrolytes and renal function, liver function tests and thyroid function.
Liver function panel

Liver function tests are in the work-up, but they look for elevation in alcoholic disease or hemochromatosis, not for anemia. Anemia is evaluated with the complete blood count. Tell: blood count for anemia; liver tests for alcohol or iron-related disease.
Thyroid function tests

Thyroid function is checked because hyperthyroidism is on the dilated cardiomyopathy differential, but it does not detect anemia. The complete blood count does. Tell: match each test to its target, and anemia belongs to the blood count.
Metabolic panel

The comprehensive metabolic panel evaluates electrolytes and renal function, not anemia. Anemia is evaluated with a complete blood count. Tell: the metabolic panel covers salts and kidneys, while anemia is read from the blood count.

set2.q: Which inheritance pattern is most common in familial dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: Mitochondrial (maternal)

Maternal mitochondrial inheritance is not the common pattern given for familial dilated cardiomyopathy. Autosomal dominant inheritance is most common in this form, which makes up to 35% of cases. Tell: the gene under study, Lamin A/C, codes proteins of the cell nucleus, not the mitochondria.
Autosomal dominant

Correct. Familial dilated cardiomyopathy accounts for up to 35% of cases, and autosomal dominant inheritance is the most common pattern. Research has focused on the Lamin A/C genotype, a gene coding proteins critical for the structure and function of the cell nucleus.
Autosomal recessive

Autosomal recessive inheritance is not the usual pattern. Familial dilated cardiomyopathy, up to 35% of cases, is most commonly autosomal dominant. Tell: many cases labeled idiopathic are likely genetic too, and the commonest inheritance remains dominant, not recessive.
X-linked recessive

X-linked recessive inheritance is not the pattern given. Familial dilated cardiomyopathy, up to 35% of cases, is most commonly autosomal dominant, with research focused on the Lamin A/C genotype. Tell: although males are affected more than females, the usual inheritance is still autosomal.

set2.q: When is anticoagulation given in Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy?
opts: Never, because recovery is usual

Recovery is usual, but that does not remove the clot risk: anticoagulation is given if a left ventricular thrombus is present. Tell: treatment depends on presentation, so a thrombus calls for anticoagulation just as heart failure calls for diuretics.
If a ventricular thrombus is present

Correct. Takotsubo treatment is empiric and supportive and depends on the presentation: anticoagulation if a left ventricular thrombus is present, diuretics if heart failure is present, and beta blockers are helpful. Patients are admitted to cardiology, and most completely recover.
For every patient at diagnosis

Anticoagulation is not universal in Takotsubo; treatment depends on presentation, and anticoagulation is given if a left ventricular thrombus is present. Tell: each supportive drug has its own trigger, a thrombus for anticoagulation and heart failure for diuretics.
Only when coronaries are blocked

Catheterization in Takotsubo most often shows normal coronary arteries, so blocked coronaries are not the trigger. Anticoagulation is given if a left ventricular thrombus is present. Tell: the indication is a clot in the ventricle, not disease in the coronary arteries.
